result.killer: No killer confirmed. The main threat is the free eCitizen societies portal, if annual returns can be filed there after login (I could not verify this). Weak willingness to pay among volunteer officers is the other.
result.reason: I found nothing that kills the idea: no vendor, association tool or consultant offers a Kenyan society Form I service. The state does run a free eCitizen societies portal (societies.ecitizen.go.ke), but its public page lists only new registrations in seven categories. Whether annual returns or change of officials can be filed after login is unsettled. The AG's notice still sends people to Sheria House, which suggests filing is manual or mixed. The duty does bite: the AG gave a 60-day window in May 2026, and a 2025 High Court case shows the Registrar demanding back returns. There are 70,000 to 100,000+ societies. But Form I is a simple form, the fee is about KSh 500 to 2,000, and officers are volunteers, so willingness to pay is weak.

result.killer: Partial: the free DOSHMIS/eCitizen portal already handles online workplace registration and renewal, including certificate download. DOSHS assigns plant examiners and receives their reports by email, so owners have little workflow to manage. No product kills it outright.
result.reason: Not refuted outright, but the core is thinner than the claim says. Annual workplace registration and renewal already run online for free on DOSHMIS: DOSHS user guides show self-assessment, eCitizen payment, certificate download and expired-certificate renewal from the portal. Whether it sends reminders is unverified, because the guide PDF would not parse. For plant examination, DOSHS's own page says it assigns workplaces to approved persons, who email scanned statutory forms to DOSHS. That leaves owners little to do and makes examiners, a small gazetted list, the likelier buyers. The 2025 fee revision is still a draft, with consultation closing 13 Oct 2025, and I found no sign it was gazetted. I found no evidence on enforcement. Generic tools (myosh, SafetyCulture) cover expiry registers, and no Kenya-specific competitor turned up.

result.killer: Possible killer, not confirmed as live: the EPRA central LPG tracking system under the Petroleum (LPG) Regulations 2025, where dealers enter sales at the point of sale and EPRA holds the database. An August 2026 report describes the rollout of serial numbers paired with EPRA seals. Also, the market is small: 459 licensed LPG cylinder retailers (The Star, June 2024).
result.reason: I found no commercial register product, but three things weaken the case. First, the 2025 LPG Regulations say dealers will enter sale details into an EPRA-run central tracking system at the point of sale, which would replace a private register. An August 2026 report says serial-number seals, plus USSD/app checks for consumers, are being rolled out. I found no confirmed go-live date. Second, the market looks small. In June 2024 EPRA counted only 459 licensed cylinder retailers, though a study using data from about 2019 cited 5,762 licensed LPG retailers. Third, enforcement looks weak. Receipts showing cylinder serial numbers have been required for years, yet unlicensed trade persists. Kiosk retailers are also unlikely to pay. The duty is real but recent, and it may be captured by the state system.

result.killer: None found. Partial threats: First AML and Realaml (law-firm KYC workflow tools from New Zealand), Sumsub/YouVerify generic KYC, and consultancies such as FNJ Associates.
result.reason: I found no product that kills this. No Kenya-specific CDD/STR/goAML tool for small estate agencies or law firms turned up. The nearest options are foreign or generic: First AML and Realaml (New Zealand, law-firm KYC, with no sign of Kenya configuration), Sumsub, YouVerify and Smile ID (aimed at banks and fintechs), and AML Guard (casinos, insurers and gaming). The duty does bite. An LSK FAQ dated August 2026 says it applies to all private-practice advocates, sole practitioners included, and the FRC has set a 2026 inspection cycle. Limits: the market is small (the FRC targeted 1,504 real estate agents, only 112 had registered at the time of reporting, and only conveyancing advocates are in scope), willingness to pay is weak, and global tools could expand into this space. I did not run Swahili queries, and the LSK FAQ was unreadable.

result.killer: None decisive. Partial substitutes: CBK's free BSA returns portal, loan-management systems such as SuperLMS that cover reporting, and law firms offering licensing work. Main risks: high fixed fees push out the smallest lenders, and licensed digital lenders are exempt from reapplying.
result.reason: No product kills it. I found no dedicated NDTCP licensing or compliance software in searches in English or Swahili. Press reports say the final rules exist as LN 191 of 2026, which gives a six-month window to about March 2027. The market is weaker than claimed for four reasons. (1) The 281 digital lenders already licensed don't need to reapply. (2) Fees are high, so the smallest lenders and chama-type lenders may stop lending rather than comply: KES 100k to apply, KES 250k a year for registration, KES 500k a year for a licence, and a KES 1m late fee. (3) Returns go through CBK's free BSA portal, and loan-management vendors already say they cover regulatory reporting. (4) Law firms already offer done-for-you licensing. The rush is a one-off; after it, the recurring work is small. I could not confirm the KES 20m threshold in the final text or the number of offline lenders.

result.competitor: I found no software or consultancy that handles TRA licensing or levy filing for hosts. Nyumbani.ke sells Airbnb and short-stay management software (invoicing, occupancy dashboards) but does not advertise TRA or levy features. The main threat is the platform deduct-and-remit model announced for June 2026. If it is live, the platforms take over the monthly levy and the host is left with only the annual TRA licence. I could not confirm whether a Tourism Fund online portal exists.
result.duty: Two duties exist on paper. (1) Licensing: since the February 2024 directive, short-term rental operators must register with the Tourism Regulatory Authority (TRA). The application fee is KES 1,000 one time, the licence is KES 26,000 per unit per year, and late payment costs 10% of the licence fee for each month. The licence is renewed yearly. NGAO/TRA inspections and CCTV were also announced (People Daily, Nation, Standard, Kenyans.co.ke, 2024). (2) Tourism levy: the Tourism Levy Order 2015 (LN 198/2015) and the Tourism Fund Regulations 2015 (LN 199/2015) set a 2% levy on monthly gross receipts from accommodation. Owners file Form TFR 1 and pay by the 10th of the following month. Late payment costs an instant KES 5,000 plus 3% of the levy due per month, and late or false returns are an offence (Kenya Law). The Tourism Fund says hosts are already covered. In January 2026 it announced platforms would collect from June 2026, with Airbnb, Booking.com and Jumia deducting and remitting at booking. No source confirms that platform collection has started. Swahili-language search was not done. I found no evidence of a guest-register rule under the Tourism Act.
result.market: Estimates of Airbnb listings in Kenya run from about 35,000 to 50,000 (Citizen: over 35,000 not paying the levy; 2023 reporting: about 40,000 listed hosts; TRA target: 50,000). Few are registered: about 400 with the Tourism Fund in 2023 and about 8,000 licensed by TRA in 2024. Many hosts own one or two units, so the number of buyers is smaller than the number of listings.
result.reason: The duties are real and in force (annual TRA licence per unit; monthly 2% levy with penalties under LN 198/199 of 2015). No compliance tool for hosts was found. Even so, the opportunity is weak. The recurring monthly part, the levy, is moving to platform deduct-and-remit, which would leave hosts with one simple annual licence payment. Enforcement is weak: about 8,000 of 35,000 to 50,000 hosts are licensed and only 400 were registered for the levy in 2023. That points to low pain and low willingness to pay. Hosts are scattered small owners who are cheap to reach through Facebook groups or property managers, but the MVP would be little more than a filing service. It might work as a feature in short-stay property-management software, not as a standalone product. The platform rollout status is unconfirmed.

result.competitor: I found no commercial cylinder-register or compliance app for LPG retailers. The English search, a Swahili search and a gas-shop POS/eTIMS search all came up empty. result.duty: Confirmed and in force. EPRA's notice 'Safety Requirements for LPG Cylinder Wholesalers and Retailers' (Feb 2026) cites the Petroleum Act and the Petroleum (LPG) Regulations 2025. The notice requires: a valid EPRA licence for retail or wholesale of LPG in cylinders; written brand-owner consent notified to EPRA; a valid fire certificate; a calibrated weighing scale; safety signage and stacking limits; a record for each cylinder sold (brand, serial number, net weight, price); and a receipt showing the cylinder's details for every sale. The duty applies to every sale, with licences renewed periodically. Penalties are prosecution, fines, suspension or revocation. No compliance deadline appears in the readable text. A secondary report says the earlier rules carried a KSh 50,000 fine for each record-keeping offence and required records to be kept for more than a year (one report says 24 months); I did not verify these against the 2025 text. The fetch of the 2025 No. 2 Regulations returned 403. The Guidelines PDF was unreadable binary, so its inspection frequency, risk tiers and record format are not_reached.
result.market: The figures conflict. The Star (June 2024), citing EPRA, puts licensed cylinder retailers at 459, with 113 licensed for storage and wholesale of cylinders. result.competitor: I found no Kenya-specific CDD/STR/goAML workflow tool for small estate agencies or law firms. Nearby options: YouVerify and Smile ID (KYC/AML aimed at banks and CBK-regulated firms), AML Guard (Nairobi, founded 2025; serves casinos, insurers and gaming), CheckLynx (sanctions screening), and consultancies such as FNJ Associates that help with FRC registration. LSK's free AML/CFT/CPF Compliance Hub offers a template policy, due-diligence guidance, STR red-flag notes, TFS circulars and a statistical questionnaire, but no software or portal. STRs are filed on the FRC's goAML portal. I did not check whether it supports XML or batch upload.
result.duty: POCAMLA 2009 as amended (2023, 2025) and the POCAMLA Regulations 2023. Real estate agents (selling, mortgaging, letting or managing immovable property) and advocates acting for clients in property, client-funds or company and trust work are reporting institutions. Duties: register with the FRC on goAML (s.47A; failing to register is an offence under s.47A(5); the agents' deadline was 14 Nov 2025 and has passed); CDD/EDD (PEPs, beneficial owners); an MLRO and internal AML system; STRs (secondary sources say within 7 working days; not confirmed from the statute); weekly Friday reports to the FRC on deals over USD 15,000, with buyer identity and source of income; 7-year record retention. Penalties: up to KSh25m for institutions, KSh5m for individuals, KSh10,000 a day for up to 180 days. LSK is the self-regulatory body for advocates. Its Legal Sector Guidelines were approved in Oct 2025, and it added a Law Firm Statistical Questionnaire in June 2026 (submitted by email as a PDF).
result.market: Estate agents: the FRC targeted 1,504 agents for registration, and 112 had registered by late Oct 2025. An undated EARB figure puts registered agents at about 3,000, and more than 40,000 unregistered agents are said to operate. Advocates: about 23,000 practising LSK members and about 27,000 enrolled (late 2025), though only those doing covered work are in scope. The claim's risk-profiled figures (153 agencies, 74 law firms rated medium/high risk) come from the cited Business Daily article, which I did not re-check.
result.reason: The duty is real and in force. Under POCAMLA s.47A, estate agents (selling, letting or managing property) and advocates are reporting institutions. They must register on goAML, carry out CDD and EDD, appoint an MLRO, file STRs, keep records for 7 years and report weekly (every Friday, per Business Daily) on property deals over USD 15,000. Fines run to KSh25m for institutions and KSh5m for individuals, plus KSh10,000 a day. I found no Kenya-specific small-firm CDD/STR tool. LSK's free hub gives template policies, guidance and a questionnaire but no software. Weak points: only 112 of 1,504 targeted agents had registered, the FRC did 44 DNFBP inspections against a target of 487, and firms seem unlikely to pay. The STR deadline is still unclear: secondary sources say 7 working days and one template says 3. Not checked: whether goAML offers XML or batch upload.

result.competitor: I found no dedicated NDTCP compliance or licensing-pack software. (2) Law firms that advise on licensing, such as Cliffe Dekker Hofmeyr, Bowmans and CM Advocates. (3) Loan-management systems that say they cover regulatory reporting, such as SuperLMS by Super Systems (Nairobi; says it serves 40 MFIs and digital lenders), Lendsqr, Presta and Craft Silicon. result.duty: Business Laws (Amendment) Act 2024 / amended CBK Act s.57; CBK (Non-Deposit Taking Credit Providers) Regulations 2026, Legal Notice 191, published 29 Sep 2026 (from secondary sources; I did not open the Kenya Law or Gazette text). They revoke the 2022 DCP Regulations. Existing lenders must apply for a licence or registration within 6 months (about 29 Mar 2027) and can keep trading while CBK decides. Lenders with KES 20m or more in capital, borrowings or loan book need a licence; smaller ones register and must convert to a licence once they pass KES 20m. Fees: KES 100k application; annual KES 500k (licensed) or KES 250k (registered), due 31 Dec. Paying within 3 months after the deadline costs double; after that CBK may revoke the licence. Other duties: CBK prior approval for new products or changes (including interest rates), complaints handling and reporting, returns via the CBK BSA system (outstanding credit returns), and an annual compliance return. Coverage includes BNPL, hire purchase, P2P, PAYG and logbook lenders. Banks, microfinance banks and SACCOs are excluded.
result.market: 281 digital credit providers were licensed as of 28 Sep 2026, and CBK has received more than 900 DCP applications since 2022. The new regime adds a pool of offline lenders: logbook lenders, shylocks, hire purchase, BNPL and PAYG. I found no count of these. The CBK regulatory impact assessment PDF could not be parsed. Realistic addressable market: a few hundred to low thousands of firms. The KES 250k annual registration fee may push many micro lenders out or underground.
result.reason: The duty is real. Secondary sources say the CBK NDTCP Regulations 2026 are Legal Notice 191, gazetted 29 Sep 2026, with Kenya Law listing them as commenced that day. Existing lenders have six months to apply, so the deadline is about 29 Mar 2027. Lenders under KES 20m register and larger ones need a licence. Annual fees are KES 250k to register and KES 500k for a licence, and late payment costs double. Other duties: CBK approval before product changes, complaints reporting, and returns filed through CBK's BSA system. I found no dedicated compliance pack. Partial substitutes exist: law firms do licensing, the CBK portal handles applications, and loan-management vendors such as SuperLMS say they produce regulator reports. Weak points: the high fees may push out the smallest informal lenders, and those lenders are hard to reach. This is a one-off rush followed by a modest recurring need.

Duty is real: the Early Childhood Education Act No. 3 of 2021 has a Part III on registering centres (provisional then full registration by the County Education Board), and counties add their own laws (Marsabit, Kisumu 2026). I could not confirm the Act's penalties, the renewal frequency or the number of centres. The Kisumu 2026 regulations are reported only in news (the Capital FM report calls the parent law the "ECD Education Act, 2023", which conflicts with 2021), and I found no fee schedule. Registration is mostly one-off, with periodic inspection, so it is weakly recurring. The market is fragmented across 47 counties, and private daycare owners are mostly informal, low-paying micro-operators. Searches found no dedicated compliance software, but only generic school-management tools were checked, and the state NEMIS and county boards were not. The score is low because the pain is episodic, the buyers are poor and the rules differ by county.

Duty is real: the Public Benefit Organizations Act 2013 is in force, and PBO Regulations 2026 (Legal Notice 43, gazetted 18 Mar 2026) require an annual report on Form 13 with a KSh 2,000 fee within six months of year end. Penalty is deregistration. PBORA has already moved to deregister 2,802 NGOs. The re-registration deadline of 13 May 2026 has passed, so that part is a one-off. The 2025 filing deadline was extended to 9 July 2026 after eCitizen payment problems. I found no PBO-specific compliance software in two searches. That is weak evidence, not proof. Market is roughly 12,000-14,000 registered NGOs, and only about 4,000 had transitioned. Weaknesses: one cheap annual form, buyers are tiny with little willingness to pay, and consultants and accountants already do the filing. The state's eCitizen portal is the filing channel.

Duty is real: EPR Regulations 2024 (LN 176/2024) require producer registration with NEMA (KES 5,000), annual licence, 4-year EPR plan, annual reports to NEMA/counties, PRO membership with fees, and KES 150 per item importer certificate. NEMA announced full enforcement in Dec 2025. No Kenyan EPR software or NEMA e-portal found (only foreign Sensoneo, aimed at PROs). But I found no small-producer threshold either way. PROs handle reporting for members, so the software need is thin. Buyers are manufacturers and importers, not quiet family firms. Industry is disputing the charges in court, and the legal basis may shift. Few recurring tasks. Fits the study focus poorly.

The duty is real. The National Transport and Safety (Operation of Commercial Vehicles) Regulations 2026 were reported in force from 1 July 2026. They require service records kept 2 years, fatal-crash reports to NTSA within 20 hours, and give NTSA power to audit maintenance and driver records. Penalty is licence revocation. I found no gazette notice, and I did not check the vehicle-size threshold or the Senate committee report. NTSA deferred enforcement of telematics (9(d)) and underride protection (9(h)). Officers check inspection stickers through the NTSA Mobile App. Fleet and telematics vendors already exist (Track n Trace, MiX Telematics). Evidence of who inspects records is weak, and no business count was found. Buyers are fragmented and the enforcement date is unclear, so pain and willingness to pay are uncertain.

The duty is real in direction but its legal status is unclear. NTSA said in 2023 that every boda rider must belong to a registered Sacco. The Nairobi 2025 Regulations appeared to be still in stakeholder consultation as of the county's April 2026 notice, and I found no gazette notice showing they are in force. The 100-member Sacco figure comes from a 2022 NTSA draft; I found no evidence it was adopted. Competition: NikoDigi (a Sacco management system with a boda product line) exists, and Mctaba describes generic transport Sacco software. Nothing found does permit compliance specifically. Market size was not found. Riders pay little and are fragmented, so the score stays low.

Duty is real: TRA registration for short-term rentals since Feb 2024 (KES 1,000 application, KES 26,000 per unit per year, 10% per month late penalty), with inspections and TRA-PSRA guest registration plans. The 2% tourism levy extension was announced early 2026, with collection at source from platforms (which shrinks the host-side duty). I could not confirm it took effect or that the June 2026 deadline was met. Market is roughly 8,000 licensed against a 50,000 target. I found no dedicated compliance software, but only 2 searches were run and no Swahili search. The duty is mostly annual, so frequency is low. Hosts are fragmented and platform remittance erodes the pain. Guest-register detail is unclear.

Duty is real but it is an EU rule, not Kenyan law. Under the Dec 2025 amendment (published OJEU 23 Dec 2025), the application date is 30 Dec 2026 for medium and large operators and 30 Jun 2027 for micro and small operators. Kenyan exporters must supply plot geolocation and legality data to EU buyers. Coverage is thin: EFI says there is no nationwide grower registry, data is fragmented across 605+ co-ops, and about 30% of farms are mapped. Competition: Tracextech sells to Kenyan coffee exporters, plus donor mapping and global EUDR tools, and I did not check Kenyan vendors. Buyers are co-ops that depend on donors, so willingness to pay is weak. The market is a few hundred co-ops plus a small number of exporters. A later EU simplification review could change the dates, and I did not check it. Score stays at 3.5.

The duty is real. Counties require an annual Single Business Permit (SBP) per outlet, with fire and health certificates. Penalties are set by county Finance Acts. Kericho's Act has 3% per month plus 30% on arrears, and the Elgeyo-Marakwet 2024 Act sets 31 March for renewals. The claim's "31 January" comes only from secondary guides, so the deadline differs by county. The pain is shrinking. Nairobi's e-Unified Business Permit (UBP) has combined business, fire, food, health and advertising permits since Jan 2024. Nakuru and Mombasa also bundle them. A County Licensing (Uniform Procedures) Act 2024 is reported in a column, which I did not verify. I found no multi-outlet or done-for-you product, and no licensing agents, but my search was thin. About 1.56M licensed MSMEs (2016 survey), but multi-outlet buyers are few. County portals are fragmented. Willingness to pay is weak.

Duty looks real: POCAMLA s.44 requires forex bureaus to report suspicious transactions to the FRC, and CBK licensing runs yearly. I only saw secondary sources (a 2012 CBK circular, CBK licensing procedures), not the 2007 regulations or the 2025 amendment. I did not verify the goAML channel. I found no bureau-specific compliance product, but only two searches were run. The CBK April 2026 directory is a PDF I couldn't parse. Its roughly 85 contact links are only a loose proxy, so about 85-90 bureaus is unconfirmed. The market is under 100 firms. Buyers are reachable through an association, but willingness to pay is likely low. Generic KYC vendors and bank systems compete. Low score because the market is tiny.
